patient.name: John Harris
patient.chiefComplaint: Confusion and diaphoresis of one hour duration, unable to answer questions

history.hpi: Patient was reportedly at his baseline this morning, took his usual morning medications, and spent the day working in his garage. He skipped lunch entirely. Approximately one hour before the 911 call his wife noticed he was confused, sweaty, and no longer making sense. He has not answered her questions since. There is no report of trauma, fall, chest pain, headache, seizure activity, or focal weakness. He is not able to give any history himself; all information comes from his wife.
history.lastOralIntake: Breakfast at approximately 8:00 AM; lunch skipped entirely, nothing by mouth since
history.events: Wife noticed progressive confusion and diaphoresis over the past hour after he came in from the garage; she was unable to get him to answer her and called 911

scene.dispatch: 68-year-old male, altered mental status, acting strangely, private residence
scene.location: Clean, well-kept single-family home; patient in the living room slumped in a recliner
scene.safety: No hazards identified; residence is orderly with clear egress
scene.bystanders: Wife, Mary, is the sole historian and met the crew at the door; she is anxious but organized and can produce the medication list
visualCues: Patient slumped in a recliner, eyes open but gaze unfocused
Visible facial and forehead diaphoresis with pale skin
Mumbling incoherently, does not track providers with his eyes
Glucometer and insulin pen visible on the kitchen counter
No pill bottles, alcohol, or paraphernalia in view

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 68-year-old male slumped in a recliner, pale and diaphoretic, mumbling incoherently and not oriented to person, place, time, or event. He does not follow commands. His airway is self-maintained and his vital signs are stable apart from tachycardia. His wife reports a one-hour history of confusion, a skipped lunch, and a nightly long-acting insulin dose.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent and self-maintained; no stridor or gurgling, no pooled secretions
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Slightly fast but of adequate depth, unlabored, symmetric chest rise
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse present, rapid and strong; skin pale, cool, and diaphoretic; no obvious bleeding
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Moves all extremities, localizes to stimulus, does not follow commands; no focal deficit appreciated
otherFindings: Not oriented to person, place, time, or event (A&O x0)
Does not track providers with his eyes
No signs of head trauma or tongue bite
No insulin pump in place; long-acting insulin is by pen injection
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: Incomprehensible mumbling only; no intelligible words

expectedActions.shortAction: Primary survey; confirm airway patency and reposition as needed
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Look for treatable causes of altered mental status (AMS): Airway: Make sure airway remains patent; reposition patient as needed. Breathing: Look for respiratory depression; check SPO2, EtCO2, and CO detector readings. Circulation: Look for signs of poor perfusion.
expectedActions.rationale: A patient who cannot follow commands is at risk of losing airway protection; airway, oxygenation, and perfusion come before the diagnostic workup.

expectedActions.shortAction: Obtain full SAMPLE history from the wife; patient cannot give one
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Key Considerations: History from bystanders and caregivers. Age of the patient. Development age and baseline functional status.
expectedActions.rationale: The wife's account of the skipped lunch and the nightly long-acting insulin is what points directly at hypoglycemia; the patient cannot supply any of it.

expectedActions.shortAction: Check blood glucose level; result is 45 mg/dL
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Performance Measures: When in scope of practice, blood glucose is checked for all patients with symptoms of altered level of consciousness, seizure, stroke, or hypoglycemia.
expectedActions.rationale: A glucometer reading is the single test that converts an undifferentiated altered mental status into a treatable diagnosis.

expectedActions.shortAction: Withhold oral glucose; patient cannot protect his own airway
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If blood glucose is 60 mg/dL or less administer one of the following: Conscious patient with a patent airway: Glucose, oral (in form of glucose tablets, glucose gel, tube of cake icing, etc.). Unconscious patient, or patients who are unable to protect their own airway: Dextrose IV.
expectedActions.rationale: Forcing oral glucose into a patient who is not oriented and will not follow commands risks aspiration; the protocol routes this patient to a parenteral option.

expectedActions.shortAction: Glucagon 1 mg IM if IV access cannot be established
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Glucagon IM/IN - an option for patients for whom IV access cannot be established. Adult dosing: 1 mg IM/IN (or prefilled 3 mg dry powder IN or prefilled IM autoinjector).
expectedActions.rationale: Glucagon is the protocol-designated route when the patient cannot take oral glucose and IV access is not obtained; it is a fixed 1 mg adult dose, not weight-based.

transitions.if: BGL checked; glucagon 1 mg IM given
transitions.condition: Crew performs a primary survey, obtains the SAMPLE history from the wife, checks a blood glucose level that returns 45 mg/dL, correctly withholds oral glucose because the patient cannot protect his airway, and administers glucagon 1 mg IM.

transitions.if: BGL not checked or oral glucose forced
transitions.condition: Crew fails to obtain a blood glucose level, does not recognize the signs of hypoglycemia, or attempts to force oral glucose into a patient who is not oriented and will not follow commands; the hypoglycemia goes uncorrected and the patient deteriorates over the next ten minutes.

phases.name: BGL checked; glucagon 1 mg IM given
phases.description: Within several minutes of the intramuscular glucagon the patient begins tracking the providers and can state his name. Over roughly fifteen minutes he becomes alert and oriented to person, place, time, and event. His skin turns pink, warm, and dry, his heart rate falls, and a repeat glucose is 110 mg/dL. He reports feeling shaky and does not remember the last hour.
phases.triggerCondition: Intramuscular glucagon mobilizes hepatic glycogen stores; serum glucose rises over 10 to 15 minutes and mental status follows, with resolution of the sympathetic response that produced the tachycardia and diaphoresis.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, self-maintained, speaking in full sentences
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse strong and regular; skin pink, warm, and dry
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Follows commands, strength symmetric, no focal deficit
otherFindings: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and event (A&O x4)
Amnestic to the period of confusion
Long-acting insulin from last night is still active
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Wow, I feel a little shaky. What happened? Mary, why are these folks here?"

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess vitals and mental status; recheck glucose after treatment
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Reassess patient: Reassess vital signs (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, neurologic status assessment) and mental status. Repeat check of blood glucose level if previous hypoglycemia and mental status has not returned to normal.
expectedActions.rationale: Documented reassessment after an intervention is how the crew proves the glucagon worked and catches a relapse early.

expectedActions.shortAction: Offer a carbohydrate and protein meal now that he can swallow
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Disposition: If symptoms of hypoglycemia resolve after treatment, release without transport should only be considered if all the following are true: Patient can promptly obtain and will eat a carbohydrate meal.
expectedActions.rationale: Glucagon depletes hepatic glycogen; without oral intake the glucose will fall again once the stores are exhausted.

expectedActions.shortAction: Strongly encourage transport; nightly Lantus is still on board
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Disposition: If hypoglycemia with continued symptoms, transport to closest appropriate receiving facility. Release without transport should only be considered if all the following are true: Repeat glucose is greater than 80 mg/dL; Patient takes insulin or metformin to control diabetes and does not take long-acting oral sulphunylurea agents.
expectedActions.rationale: The glucagon effect is transient while the long-acting insulin is not; this is the release-criteria discussion the scenario is built around.

transitions.condition: Crew documents reassessment of vital signs, mental status, and repeat glucose, provides a complex carbohydrate and protein source, walks the patient and his wife through the release criteria, and the patient accepts transport for evaluation of the recurrent hypoglycemia risk.

phases.name: Reassessed; transport accepted
phases.description: The patient remains alert and oriented with normal skin signs and a stable glucose. He has eaten and has accepted transport. The crew hands off with a documented pre- and post-treatment glucose, the reassessment findings, and the identified cause of the episode.
phases.triggerCondition: After reassessment, oral intake, and a clear explanation of why the glucagon effect will not outlast the nightly insulin dose, the patient and his wife agree to transport for further evaluation.

clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse strong and regular; skin pink, warm, and dry
otherFindings: A&O x4 and stable through transport
Has eaten a sandwich provided by his wife
Clear cause identified: skipped lunch with long-acting insulin on board
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I feel a lot better. I guess I should have stopped for lunch."

phases.name: BGL not checked or oral glucose forced
phases.description: Roughly ten minutes from initial contact the mumbling stops. The patient now responds only to painful stimulus with a groan. His respirations are slow and shallow, his pulse is thready, and his skin is very clammy. A glucose checked at this point reads 30 mg/dL. He is at high risk for seizure and airway loss.
phases.triggerCondition: The blood glucose was never obtained, the hypoglycemia was not recognized, or oral glucose was pushed on a patient who could not protect his airway; with no effective treatment the serum glucose continues to fall and cerebral function declines.

clinicalPresentation.airway: At risk; no longer reliably self-maintained, requires positioning and monitoring for secretions
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Shallow and slow at 10/min, decreased tidal volume
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulse rapid and thready; skin increasingly pale and very clammy
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Withdraws from painful stimulus only; no purposeful movement
otherFindings: Responds to sternal rub with a groan only
Blood glucose 30 mg/dL if checked at this point
Ventilation now inadequate; assisted ventilation may be required
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: No intelligible speech; groans to painful stimulus

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize deterioration; support ventilation and check glucose now
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patient Safety Considerations: With depressed mental status, initial focus is on airway protection, oxygenation, ventilation, and perfusion.
expectedActions.rationale: At a respiratory rate of 10 with shallow depth this patient is hypoventilating; the airway and breathing must be addressed alongside the glucose correction.

expectedActions.shortAction: Glucagon 1 mg IM now, or D10% 250 mL IV if access is obtained
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Unconscious patient, or patients who are unable to protect their own airway: Dextrose IV - administer in incremental doses until mental status improves or maximum field dosing is reached (if available, D10% is preferred). Maximum field adult dosing: 25 g of 10-50% dextrose IV; 250 mL of 10% dextrose. Glucagon IM/IN - an option for patients for whom IV access cannot be established. Adult dosing: 1 mg IM/IN.
expectedActions.rationale: Correcting the glucose is still the only treatment that reverses this presentation; the delay has narrowed the margin, not changed the therapy.

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate rapid transport for refractory hypoglycemia
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If maximal field dosage of dextrose solution does not achieve euglycemia and normalization of mental status: Initiate transport to closest appropriate receiving facility for further treatment of refractory hypoglycemia. Evaluate for alternative causes of altered mental status.
expectedActions.rationale: Prolonged neuroglycopenia risks permanent injury; this patient needs definitive care regardless of the field response.
